memory_verse.label: Bible Reference
memory_verse.text: "'Now then, your two sons born to you in Egypt before I came to you here will be reckoned as mine; Ephraim and Manasseh will be mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine.'" — Gen 48:5 (NIV)

devotion.label: Devotion
devotion.text:
This is a formal act of adoption, and it changes everything for these two young men. Ephraim and Manasseh were Joseph's sons — half-Egyptian, born to the daughter of an Egyptian priest, raised in a foreign court. Now Jacob says: they will be reckoned as mine, just as Reuben and Simeon are mine.

Just as. Not slightly less than. Not honorary members with limited privileges. They are placed on exactly the same footing as Jacob's own firstborn sons, with a full tribal inheritance each.

Everything about their birth said outsider. One word from the father says son.

That word — adoption — is one of the most beautiful in the New Testament. Paul says we received the Spirit of sonship, by whom we cry "Abba, Father" (Rom 8:15). We were outsiders too, by birth and by choice, with no natural claim on God's family. And in Christ we are not made almost-children or probationary members. We are heirs of God and co-heirs with Christ.

Whatever your background says about you, your Father's word about you is stronger. He has said: mine.

reflection.label: Reflection
reflection.text:
1. Do you live as a full child of God, or as though you are on probation?
2. What in your past makes you feel like an outsider?
3. What difference would it make today to hear God say "mine" over you?

prayer.label: Prayer
prayer.text: Father, thank You that You have adopted me fully in Christ, not partly and not on trial. Help me live today as Your child and not as an outsider. Amen.
